content.thinking:
I'm checking how other samples handle geometry merging with null-safe type handling, then writing helper functions for vector construction and position/rotation transforms.

Still writing transform helpers...

Now I'm setting up joint definitions for the hoard's core structure, starting with the root spine and a hinged lid joint.

I'm figuring out the correct type imports for Fill, Paint, and Joint, making sure to pull Joint and related types from the skeleton module and Paint as a type-only import.

Writing the put helper function...

Defining height function...

Now I'm designing a coin placement function that computes position and orientation, then grouping coin geometries into buckets by tone so I can batch them efficiently -- building cylinder geometries oriented via quaternion rotation from the up axis to the surface normal.

Still writing coin logic...

For stacked coins I'm computing base heights from the mound slope, adding slight jitter and random rotation, alternating tones, with roughly four stacks of 6-12 coins. I'm sketching coin counts overall, around 380 scattered plus 40 stacked, then planning a separate textured hero coin as a cylinder body.

For the hero coin I'm defining a gold-colored body with front and back circle faces positioned slightly leaning against the mound, computing its orientation by blending the surface normal with a tilt vector so it faces outward naturally.

I'm scattering nine coins across chosen front-facing floor coordinates, clamping their height above the surface so none sink below ground, then moving on to define the chest's outer dimensions as constants for its geometry.

Still writing chest geometry...

Lining heights span 0.05 to 0.45, centered at y=0.25 with 0.4 height, flush with the rim. Now I'm sizing the interior mound to sit just inside the lining bounds, and working out gold rim trim pieces that cover the tops of each wall.

I'm realizing the hinge position needs adjusting since the lid closes at y=0.485, not 0.45, so the hinge joint and barrel cylinders should be placed there, split between root and lid knuckles for the rotation.

Now I'm computing the arch-shaped outline points for the lid by sweeping an elliptical angle from near π to near 0, deriving u (depth offset) and v (height) coordinates for each sample point.

Then I'm setting up the extrusion for the lid along the X axis, positioning it near the hinge with a thickness slightly wider than the body and a small bevel. For the wood texture, I'm computing a plank angle around a reference point based on the lid's local surface coordinates so the grain pattern follows the arch curvature, applying the same mapping to the extruded end faces.

Placing more trim pieces...

Solving the ellipse equation to find where the arch surface sits at that v-coordinate, I get u≈0.687, putting the plate near the vertical front edge of the discretized arch polygon. I'm working out the z-offset to place the gold backing box flush against that face.

I'm positioning the lock plate, hasp, and keyhole geometry: a textured lock plane with LOCK texture facing outward, a hasp box on the body front with a ring detail, and a glowing cyan gem (octahedron) centered on the lid plate for the key highlight. I'm thinking through how the hasp should look once the lid is open, keeping the body-side plate with its keyhole texture intact while the lid-side lock plate lifts away.

Let me adjust the LOCK plate to center at y=0.27 with a height spanning 0.16 to 0.38, and have the tongue span from 0.36 to 0.52 so it overlaps correctly between lid and body, with a small gem hanging at its base. I'm checking that the front mound doesn't collide with this area, confirming it stops around y=0.14 while the lock plate starts at 0.16, so there's clearance.

Now I'm sizing glowing rune strips on the front wall, fitting them between the metal straps and the lock plate so they occupy the 0.16-to-0.285 gap without overlapping, keeping their height low enough to avoid the mound. For the straps themselves, I'm figuring out whether to extend them as full-depth plates wrapping over the lid and body, making sure they don't poke through the floor or collide with the rim trim near the top.

Then I'm placing small gold studs along each strap at regular vertical intervals on the front faces, adding corner posts as tall gold boxes at the four sides sized to stop just below the rim trim, and deciding to skip separate feet since the body already sits flush on the floor.

Next I'm adding a dark steel bottom plinth box beneath the body as a base trim, then creating side handles from a torus ring rotated to face outward with a backing plate, both gold, before starting hinge knuckles as small cylinders along the back top edge.

I'm placing three hinge knuckle cylinders at the back top with the center one for the lid and the outer two anchored to the body, then adding a glowing cyan crystal cluster peeking above the interior coin mound for a strong lit accent visible when the lid is open, and finally sketching a quilted lining panel for the underside of the lid.

For the lining plate, I work out its exact vertical placement so it protrudes slightly below the lid's bottom face without clashing badly with the hinge rim trim — a small 3mm overlap into the trim volume is acceptable since the geometry doesn't actually collide. When the lid swings open 105°, this plate reads as the quilted interior lining, which looks right. Now I'm starting on a raised medallion decoration for the top of the lid.

For the medallion itself, I'm calculating where the flat facet at the peak of the arched lid sits (around y=0.7616) and checking whether a 0.1-radius disc fits on that facet or spills slightly onto the adjacent sloped facets — it does spill a little, but only onto a shallow ~9° slope, so I'm positioning the disc center there anyway.

Adjusting so the disc sits snug instead of floating, centering it at y=0.7596, and now thinking about adding a crest texture as a small circle plane positioned just above the disc, oriented facing upward.

Since the lid stays open, the medallion mostly stays hidden from the front view, with only the interior and exterior-from-behind visible. I'll move on to positioning crown details, then build a cluster function for generating crystal and rock formations.

Still writing cluster logic...

Shaping the crystal profile so the hexagonal lathe closes cleanly along the axis with flat-shaded facets, then considering whether the rock base should use a flattened hemisphere geometry.

For the stone material I'm writing a paint function that blends deep purple to lighter violet based on lighting and noise, occasionally brightening toward cyan-flecked specks. I'm also designing a cut-gem lathe profile with a pointed pavilion, wide girdle, and flat table top, placing these gems tilted randomly across the rock's surface with a glowing emissive quality.

Now I'm working out gem sizing (girdle radius scaling from total height) and planning a rejection-sampling approach to scatter roughly 22 gems across the front of the mound, avoiding overlap with the crown and goblet positions using distance checks against an avoidance registry. I'm also starting to lay out the goblet positions in the scene's top-down coordinate system.

I'm mapping the full layout now: establishing screen-right/+X and toward-viewer/+Z conventions, then placing the chest, crystal clusters, mounds (center, left, right, front-left, front-right crown), and a spill feature along the front rim with specific coordinates and dimensions for each.

Checking the spill coins coming over the front wall against the rim height — they roughly match, so I can position E to let coins cascade from the interior pile down over the wall to M1, settling on coordinates that put its top just under the rim.

Now I'm checking whether the ML/MR side mounds near the chest overlap into the chest footprint — testing a sample point at MR confirms the height there drops below 0.5, so it's correctly excluded from the interior region. I also verify ML's z-span reaches close to cluster A, and note a crown position on MFR with a low height value there.

For the goblets, I'm placing G1 upright near the ML/MFL boundary where the height is low, so I'll surround its base with coins; G2 upright on the right side gets a valid height from MR of about 0.23; and G3 is tipped over lying on the floor in front of M1 since the mound height there comes out negative, meaning no mound coverage.

I'm working out the tipped goblet's orientation—angling its axis so the cup rim and foot disc both touch the floor, with the mouth opening angled toward the camera's right-front and a trail of spilled coins leading back up toward the mound.

I realize it's simpler to handle rotation via a quaternion-based transform function that aims the local Y axis toward a direction vector, so I'll extend my transform helper to accept a quaternion directly for tilting the goblet at a slight angle.

Checking the math for a tipped goblet: at a small tilt angle, I'm computing where the foot bottom sits relative to the floor and where the rim ends up, trying to find an angle small enough that the goblet's foot stays nearly flush with the ground while the bulge still looks naturally tilted.

For the spilled treasure, I'm laying out coins and gems scattered along the direction the goblet mouth points, extending outward from the rim with some lateral spread, placing each coin's height from the floor height function plus a tiny offset so they rest naturally on the terrain.

Now I'm defining how to fill each goblet: G1 gets a glowing cyan liquid disc near the rim, and G2 gets a heap of small glowing gem octahedra at varying positions and heights with a few coins tucked in among them for visual interest.

For positioning everything correctly, I need the goblet's local transform (position and rotation quaternion), with the liquid cylinder aligned along the y-axis. I'm also adding a thin gold torus ring around the goblet's rim, rotated 90 degrees to lie flat, using a helper that builds quaternions from Euler angles for these local rotations.

Now I'm placing a ring of six small octahedron gems around the goblet at a fixed radius, each oriented to point outward using an aim function, flattened slightly like cabochons to sit against the curved surface.

For the crown I'm working through the ermine ring, velvet cap, and gold band with diamond engraving, then setting eight alternating sapphire and ruby gems into the band plus a larger central cyan-blue hex gem at the front with a gold bezel torus, and planning small pearl tips for each of the eight spires.

Adding crown arches and apex orb...

I'm computing the terrain height at that position to set the base elevation, then laying out three ingots in a bottom row with slight x offsets, oriented so their length runs along z and thickness along x.

For the stacked rows above, I'm placing two ingots and then one on top, rotating the whole pile slightly around Y for a natural scattered look, and sinking the base into the mound surface. Now I'm working out positions for coin stacks near the front edge.

Adding sparkle highlights, then moving to the coin texture SVG with a radial gradient for a golden glow effect...

Still writing hexagon star shape...

Adding keyhole and rivet details...

Designing the crest...

Now I'm sketching a simple star-burst spark icon for the SPARK element, then moving on to defining shading helper functions for the paint/color bands used across the icons.

Still tuning shading logic...

Now I'm defining a wood paint function that differs by usage: plain box bodies use seams based on vertical position with a fract threshold, while lids use stretched noise for grain, scaled differently on each axis.

Switching to a module-level scratch vector to avoid per-texel allocations, I'm picking warm brown-purple wood tones (base, light, dark, seam colors) and blending them based on grain noise and a lit dot product against a key light direction, brightening or darkening the tone depending on that lighting value.

For the lid I'm mapping local extrude coordinates into an angle to create radial seam lines around the panel, and for a quilted diamond pattern I'm computing diagonal coordinates from the dominant surface axes so seams fall where fractional diagonal distances get near zero, using a crimson base with lighter banding toward the center.

Still writing quilt shading...

For ermine fur I'm reusing a spot pattern helper with cream and dark coloring, and starting on a dark steel banded pattern for the plinth base.

Setting up a conditional paint that switches between a warmer lit scales texture and a cooler shadowed variant based on surface normal, then building each mound as a half-sphere with scale and position parameters.

Now I'm planning the coin sampling for the interior mound, defining the target region and iterating sample attempts to place roughly 420 coins within the bounds.

I'll add exclusion radii around goblets, crowns, and ingots so coins don't overlap those objects, then set up coin placement with tilted axes—most lying flat on the mound surface, a quarter standing upright—with centers nudged slightly above the analytic surface height to avoid clipping into the mesh.

I'm varying coin radii between 0.045 and 0.058, assigning lighter tones to upward-facing coins for a lit look, and keeping each coin at 32 triangles via an 8-sided cylinder, totaling around 16.6k triangles for all coins.

I'm tallying mound spheres at roughly 192 triangles each across seven mounds, then listing out sparkle positions by hand: the crown tip, gem clusters, goblet liquid, interior crystals, and loose gems, about a dozen total. I'm also checking that the cards function signature correctly accepts frame inputs and texture parameters with options like size, lean, and cross flags.

Now I'm defining the crystal clusters by color palette and position: an icy blue-cyan cluster on the back left, a purple-pink cluster on the back right, and a small interior cyan cluster sitting on the coin pile, each with its own set of gem colors and radii.

Still generating crystal placement values...

Now I'm working out the open chest lid geometry, rotating the lid arch by about 105 degrees around its hinge so the front edge swings up, giving an overall scene height near 1.2 meters.

Checking overall chest bounding dimensions, depth extends to about -1.0 with total depth near 2.1 and width 2.3, which looks fine, and the crystal clusters at x±0.95 shouldn't collide with the lid's back bulge within ±0.57. I'm also confirming the lowest points all touch the floor properly, though I notice the lid band's underside bottom face is coplanar with the lid bottom, which could cause z-fighting between those surfaces.

The lining plate protrudes enough to cover that z-fighting zone within x±0.54, and the bands at x=±0.33 are safely inside that coverage, though I need to check the band outline edges extending past the lid boundary where there's no lining to hide the overlap. With the rig simplified to just root and lid joints for a prop, I'm now starting to write the actual TypeScript code, setting up imports for Three.js utilities and the builder module.

Adding more imports...

Defining the build function with a builder config, deciding on paint resolution (opting for the default 1024 texel sheet rather than 2048 to keep the atlas manageable), then setting up the random seed and root joint for the hoard.

Writing part placement helpers...

Worried about exactOptionalPropertyTypes breaking things if I pass explicit undefined fields, so I'm restructuring to conditionally assign only defined properties onto a typed options object instead.

Then I'm setting up geometry helpers for shapes like cylinders, boxes, spheres, and tori, plus coin-related infrastructure including color tone buckets and geometry groupings for building the coin visuals.

Writing coin placement logic...

Gem height sits slightly above the surface so coins pile around and partially bury its base, which looks fine. I'm writing a helper function for sampling mound positions with minimum height and clearance constraints, then looping it inline for each object type before moving on to placing the crown.

Now I'm scattering coins around the base using random angular distribution with square-root radius weighting for even density, dropping each coin at the terrain height with a tilted axis so most lie flat with occasional ones standing upright for variety.

I'm choosing coin tones based on weighted probabilities biased toward lighter colors for upward-facing coins, then writing a stacking function that builds neat coin towers at a given base height with slight random jitter in position and alternating tones per layer.

Writing helper functions for boxes and cylinders...

I realize I can skip the separate floor box since the plinth already covers that area solidly, with its top at y=0.07. The mound's base sits higher at y=0.2, leaving a gap of empty space between the plinth top and the mound bottom that I need to account for.

Checking the mound's footprint, it spans nearly to the walls with only a narrow gap, so the hidden underside isn't really visible from above. Now I'm working out the wall placement -- they need to sit above the plinth, spanning from y=0.07 to 0.45, making sure the outer faces align properly with the plinth edges before I define each wall's box dimensions.

Placing linings...

Still placing rim trim and studs...

Now I'm sizing the lock plate backing box and checking its vertical span lines up with the mound front center height.

I should pull the tongue forward to z=0.02 so it sits clearly in front of the lock plate's texture layer, and add a small glowing cyan gem octahedron near the top of the tongue for detail.

Checking the rune panel placement too — they should float just slightly off the wood face at z=0.003, away from the lock plate backing and straps. Now I'm sketching out the lid geometry, starting with the outline function and arc construction for the extruded arch shape.

Still writing extrusion params...

Still placing lid decorations...

That overlap is only exposed when the lid is open, so it's fine to leave as is. The lid pose rotation needs to be applied after all child parts are built so they inherit the rigid transform correctly, and I'm double-checking the hinge bone direction and position are consistent with the closed-lid coordinate space. Now I'm setting up the crown construction with its transform.

Computing crown placement...

Going with 10 segments for a faceted crown band look. Now I'm defining the gold paint function to add engraved diamond patterns based on height along the band's surface, using the unscaled y-coordinate from the lathe outline as the reference.

Working out the triangular engraving pattern across the gem band, mapping angular position into repeating triangle segments and blending between a dark gold accent and the base gold depending on height within the band. Now moving on to placing eight spires around the crown, computing each spire's angular position and local offset.

Still writing spire geometry...

I'm placing octahedron gems along the spire, sizing and positioning them to fit the spire's tapering width and alternating ruby/sapphire coloring, then adding a small pearl sphere at the very tip.

Now I'm adding band gems between the spires at offset angles, scaling octahedrons and aiming them radially outward with alternating cabochon colors, then designing a larger front-center bezel gem at the main-facing angle.

I'm now planning the four decorative arches, positioning their bases on the band aligned with alternating spires and sketching the catmull curve path each arch follows upward.

Then I'm sweeping a six-sided gold tube along that path for the arch geometry, and starting to construct a velvet cap dome using a half-sphere shape for the crown's top.

Now I'm working out the ermine ring as a horizontal torus positioned near the band's base, scaling its dimensions with k so it sits slightly larger and puffier than the band, then painting ermine spots onto its surface before moving on to the apex.

For the apex, I'm placing a small gold orb sphere at the top, then adding an octahedron crystal stretched vertically above it with a cyan glow, deciding to skip extra decorative rings and tassels for simplicity. I'm also reconsidering crest placement — ruling out putting it on the crown band since it conflicts with the main front gem, settling on using the crest only on the lid medallion instead.

Now I'm starting the goblet function definition, setting up parameters for fill type, tag, and gem tones before laying out the profile points scaled appropriately.

Writing goblet paint logic...

I'm reasoning through the lathe outline coordinates to figure out which wall is the outer bowl surface, checking normal directions against the up vector so the engraved pattern only appears on the correct outward-facing wall, and confirming the geometry works out with a normal dot product around -0.25.

Now I'm positioning a glowing liquid cylinder inside the goblet bowl, computing the inner wall radius at the liquid's y-level by interpolating between outline points, and shrinking the liquid radius slightly so it doesn't clip through the inner wall.

Then I'm scattering 7-9 small octahedron "gems" across the cup bottom with randomized angle, radius, height, size, rotation, and color from a gem palette, plus adding one coin tilted at an angle sticking out of the pile for visual interest.

Now I'm placing the gold rim torus around the cup opening, then adding rings of tiny gems around the knob and bowl sections to decorate the goblet's stem. For tipped goblets I'm using a quaternion aim-based transform to orient everything along the tilt direction instead of straight upright.

For the third goblet I'm working out a position lying tipped toward the front-right, calculating the foot base and mouth opening coordinates so the interior faces the viewer while keeping the geometry grounded.

I'm checking the mound height at the foot location to see if it's buried too deeply or floating above the coin surface, and considering raising the foot slightly so it looks naturally supported by the coins rather than sinking in or hovering.

Let me try a simpler layout instead: placing the goblet entirely on the floor, closer to the front, so its base and mouth positions clear the hoard's depth range without overlap issues.

I'll settle on foot at (-0.62, 0.1, 0.9) with mouth near (-0.44, 0.12, 1.16), accepting it rests partially sunk into the mound at that point since that reads as realistic for a goblet nestled in coins. Now I'm working out the coin spill trail direction from the mouth, adjusting the lateral spread so it doesn't extend too far forward.

Checking distances from G1's new position to the other items—mug legs, M1—to confirm clearance, then verifying G1's base height sits properly on the surface near the ingots.

I'm now placing G2 and the crown, then plotting the hero coins and coin stacks relative to the tipped goblet's spill trail, making sure nothing overlaps. I'm also setting exclusion radii for each object (crown, goblets, ingots, stacks, tipped foot) so the random coin scatter avoids collisions.

I'm sampling 20 gem positions via rejection sampling within the scene bounds while respecting height, chest footprint, avoid zones, and minimum spacing, plus a few extra gems along the spill trail. Then I'm setting the crown's tilt rotation and deriving sparkle positions from a subset of the gems, checking that the card and path APIs accept the data shapes I'm using.

Now I'm writing a helper that generates clustered rocks and crystal shards around a point, placing hemisphere stones at offset positions and lathing faceted crystal shapes with varied heights, colors, and glow strength...

The bevel seems small enough to be fine. For the crystal look, I'll keep a single color with glow and let faceting vary through lighting rather than adding a separate bright tip shard, and I'll use the tones list to give some clusters a lighter hue for variation. For base placement, I'm positioning it relative to the cluster center with a slight vertical offset below the top.

Now I'm defining a lighting direction vector and a banded paint function that samples noise to shade crystals into shine, highlight, mid, shadow, and cool-shadow bands based on how lit each point is -- I'll use this to create a gold-toned material variant.

Next I'm building a wood-grain paint function that checks for seam lines to darken them, then blends brown wood-grain colors using noise, brightening lit faces toward amber and darkening shaded ones toward purple-black, making sure the types for the coordinate/normal/seam callback and color mixing stay consistent.

I'm defining seam-detection logic for the body, sides, and lid faces based on periodic position patterns, then writing a quilted-fabric paint function that projects each face onto a 2D grid, computes diagonal diamond distances to classify seam lines, puffed regions, and base fabric color.

Now I'm setting up specific material paints: a crimson quilt paint with seam/puff/base colors, a stone paint that blends purple tones based on noise and lighting direction, and starting a gradient-based "mound" paint using warm gold/orange scale colors.

Adding ermine spots, a banded plinth pattern, and verifying the lathe function signature for assembling the final mesh.

For gemstones, I'm sketching out a color palette and thinking through whether to build the gem geometry with a lathe cut or a basic cylinder shape.

Actually, THREE.LatheGeometry is the simplest solution -- spinning a profile of points around the Y axis gives a faceted brilliant-cut gem shape, with the point order going from the bottom pavilion tip upward. Then I'll place each gem using the cut geometry with the right color, position, orientation toward its axis, and a slight glow.

Now I'm working out gem placement so the pavilion tip sits just above the surface height with the orientation jittered slightly from the normal, checking that tilt doesn't drop the gem below the surface given its small width. I also need a dropGem function for spilled gems, then move on to defining the ingot outline shape and figuring out how to orient its thickness and length directions when the ingot stack is rotated around Y.

I'm laying out the ingot stack rows with small x/y offsets per layer, computing the base height from the terrain sample at that position, and setting thickness and bevel values so adjacent ingots have a slight visible gap. I'm also sanity-checking that the mound height near that stack location is reasonable before moving on to how coins get sampled.

Now I'm defining a hero coin generator function that places a tilted coin at a given terrain position: computing the coin's leaning axis from lean/azimuth angles, adjusting its vertical position so it rests properly on the ground without clipping, then placing a cylinder for the coin body and a slightly smaller circle decal on its face for the embossed design.

I'm checking the math for a coin standing nearly on edge — making sure its lowest point doesn't dip below the terrain surface when leaning 65-80 degrees from vertical — and confirming the face texture orientation stays upright relative to world up when the coin leans.

I'm placing a group of hero coins at varying lean angles (55-75°) in front, using circle geometry for the faces with a tiny z-offset to avoid flickering, then moving on to set up the cluster of hextech crystals near the chest position.

I'm deciding to skip giving unique names to most generated parts since duplicates probably aren't an issue, and confirming triangle counts should stay manageable with flat shading and texture planes applied cleanly.

For merging geometries, I'm checking that studs and coin buckets use consistent attributes so `mergeGeometries` won't return null, and planning to guard against that case before calling `put`. I'm also verifying the lid's pose rotation and bone weighting setup work correctly in model space before finalizing the return of the root bone.

Now I'm laying out the build order: declaring constants, joints, and helpers first, then mounds, the chest body and lid, then all the coin-related infrastructure (crown, goblets, crystals, gems, ingots, stacks, hero coins, scatter coins) merged into buckets at the end, followed by sparkles, posing, and returning the result. I'm defining position constants upfront so avoid zones are available before they're needed, then starting to write the transform helper type.

Writing transform helper code...

Now sketching the goblet profile points for its lathe geometry.

Checking the coordinates confirms the inner curve stays above the outer boundary at each sampled x-value, so the bowl thickness holds up without crossing itself, and the final segment just closes back down to the axis.

Now I'm writing the goblet rendering function that handles fill states for liquid, gems, or empty.

Still placing rings and gems...

Skipping the pearl base row for now, I'll move to writing the full final code, double-checking that the `aim` function's tuple argument typing is correct.

I'm adding an octahedron helper and setting up a random sampling loop to place gem spots on the surface, rejecting candidates that fall too close to the chest region, overlap existing gems, or sit on invalid height terrain.

Scattering coins...

The order of random calls only matters for determinism, which checks out. I'm defining the chest interior zone boundaries so coins stay out of the front wall region, while allowing the E spill area to extend slightly beyond those bounds.

Since interior coin spawns need a minimum height near the top of the pile, that zone is fairly small and sparse compared to the rest, so I'll add a dedicated loop of around 70 coins sampling specifically within that interior area to keep the pile looking dense there too. I also want to make sure crystal placements avoid overlapping with these interior coins.

With roughly 560 coins plus crystals and other decorative elements, I estimate the triangle count stays reasonable around 18k, so I'm fine proceeding to write the final code. I'm also verifying type compatibility across the extrude functions for the arch and spire outlines, confirming the bevel sizing logic works for the spire's sharp corners, and checking the wood seam function's parameter types align with the surface coordinate imports.

Now I'm writing the paint function for the crown's lathe band engraving, using the surface coordinates to create alternating gold and brown segments that simulate carved banding around the circumference, while also confirming the crown spire sits at the right height to overlap with the band below it.

I'm also sketching out the coin-dropping logic, where each coin gets a randomized rotation axis based on its surface normal, with a chance of standing upright versus lying flat, plus some randomized radius variation for visual diversity.

That gives scattered floor coins lying flat near the spill area. I should also verify the normal at flat floor regions resolves to pointing straight up where height is zero on all neighbors. Now I'll write out the full implementation.
